## Objectives

- Take a contingency table and turn it into a **map**
- Understand what the map shows — and the one thing it does not
- Read a perception map aloud: brands as customers see them, hospitals as patients describe them
- Lab: from a raw survey file to the map, in the second half

## Why a manager cares

::: {.subtitle-frame}
"Where do we sit in their heads?" — customers', or patients'
:::

| | You ask | You get |
|---|---|---|
| **Brand manager** | 1 200 people: which words go with each brand? *reliable, cheap, innovative, …* | brands × attributes, counts |
| **Hospital network director** | the patient-experience survey: which words describe your stay? *short wait, kind staff, …* | hospitals × words, counts |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,53,25]"}

- The question is not *which word is most common* — it is **who is close to which words, and to whom**

Correspondence analysis draws that table as a picture. It is PCA for counts: the standard tool of brand positioning, and a fast first read of a patient survey.

## [Section 1]{.section-kicker} From a table to distances {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## The table, and what "close" should mean

| | Reliable | Cheap | Innovative | Premium |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Brand A | 320 | 40 | 210 | 180 |
| Brand B | 90 | 410 | 60 | 20 |
| Brand C | 150 | 60 | 380 | 150 |
| Brand D | 260 | 30 | 110 | 350 |

Two brands are *similar* if their **row profiles** — the counts divided by the row total — are similar. Not the raw counts: B collected 580 mentions and D 750, and that alone means nothing.

A: (.43, .05, .28, .24). D: (.35, .04, .15, .47). Similar on *reliable*, apart on *premium*.

## The chi-square distance

Between two row profiles $r_i$ and $r_{i'}$, with $c_j$ the column's overall share:

$$
d^2(i, i') \;=\; \sum_{j} \frac{(r_{ij} - r_{i'j})^2}{c_j}
$$


- Euclidean distance between profiles, **weighted by $1/c_j$**: a difference on a *rare* attribute counts more than on a common one
- *Innovative* said of one brand informs, *reliable* said of every brand does not; *short wait* said of one hospital tells you more than *kind staff* said of all

::: {.callout-note}
Total inertia is $\chi^2 / n$ from the independence test: CA decomposes exactly the departure from independence.
:::

## Then PCA, on those distances

- Rows placed in a space where distances are chi-square distances
- Find the directions of greatest spread — the **axes**, as in PCA
- Do the same for columns
- Draw both on the first two axes: **the map**

Rows near each other: similar profiles. Columns near each other: attributes that go together. That much is exact.

## [Section 2]{.section-kicker} Reading the map {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## What the map shows

- **Brand–brand distance**: real. Two brands close together are perceived alike.
- **Attribute–attribute distance**: real. *Cheap* and *for students* near each other are associated in people's minds.
- **Direction from the origin**: a brand out along the *premium* side is over-associated with premium relative to average.
- **The origin** is the average profile — a brand at the centre is *undifferentiated*, which is usually the worst place to be.

## What the map does not show

::: {.subtitle-frame}
The misreading in every third marketing deck
:::

- **Brand-to-attribute distance is not a distance.** Rows and columns live in different spaces, overlaid for convenience. Brand A "next to" *innovative* is suggestive, not measured.
- The honest version: look at the *angle* from the origin. A brand and an attribute in the same direction are associated; at 90°, unrelated; opposite, anti-associated.
- Two axes may explain 60% of inertia. The other 40% is not on the page.

::: {.callout-important title="Attention"}
Never present a CA map without the percentage of inertia on each axis. A map that explains 35% of the table is a sketch, and should be called one.
:::

## In R

```{.r code-line-numbers="1|3-5|7|9|11"}
library(FactoMineR); library(factoextra)

tab <- as.table(rbind(A = c(320, 40, 210, 180), B = c(90, 410, 60, 20),
                      C = c(150, 60, 380, 150), D = c(260, 30, 110, 350)))
dimnames(tab)[[2]] <- c("Reliable", "Cheap", "Innovative", "Premium")

chisq.test(tab)                    # is there anything to map at all?

ca <- CA(tab, graph = FALSE)

fviz_ca_biplot(ca, repel = TRUE)   # the perception map
```

`ca$eig` gives inertia per axis. Put the two percentages on the plot's axis labels before anyone sees it.

## Reading our four brands

- Axis 1 separates **Cheap** (B, alone) from everything else — the value/premium divide. It carries 77% of the inertia.
- Axis 2 (19%) separates **Innovative** (C) from **Premium** (D) — the two ways of not being cheap
- A sits between C and D and near *Reliable*: solid, differentiated on nothing in particular
- B owns *cheap* and nothing else — which is a position, and a fragile one

Those four sentences are the analysis. The map exists so a marketing director can check them in ten seconds.

## [Drill 1]{.drill-kicker} Four hospitals, as their patients describe them

::: {.subtitle-frame}
In pairs · 10 minutes · `CA()` on an invented survey: 4 hospitals × 5 words
:::

| Hospital | Dim 1 (74.1%) | Dim 2 (25.7%) | Word | Dim 1 | Dim 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Centre | −0.46 | 0.10 | Short wait | 0.73 | 0.40 |
| Coast | 0.64 | 0.30 | Kind staff | 0.22 | −0.02 |
| North | 0.20 | −0.40 | Clear explanations | 0.20 | −0.42 |
| South | 0.01 | 0.01 | Expert doctors | −0.40 | 0.06 |
| | | | Modern equipment | −0.48 | 0.13 |

1. Name the contrast on each axis, in the words' own language
2. South sits at the origin. What does that tell its director?
3. Coast's report: "waiting times are short". Does the map support it? Write the sentence it does.

## [Drill 1 · answer]{.drill-kicker} What the map lets a director say

- **Axis 1 (74%)**: *Expert doctors*, *Modern equipment* — Centre, the teaching hospital — against *Short wait* — Coast. Technique against access
- **Axis 2 (26%)**: *Short wait* (Coast) against *Clear explanations* (North): two different ways patients like a hospital
- **South at the origin**: its patients describe it like the network's average hospital — no word over-said, none missing. Not good, not bad: *average*, whatever the network's average is

::: {.callout-tip title="A sentence that defends it"}
"Of our four hospitals, Coast is the one patients most associate with short waits: 31% of its mentions, against 12% across the network. How short the waits are, this survey cannot say."
:::

## [Section 3]{.section-kicker} Lab {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## From a survey file to the map

`brands.csv` on Blackboard: one row per mention — `respondent`, `brand`, `attribute`. 1 200 respondents, each describing one brand with one to three attributes: 2 356 rows.

```{.r code-line-numbers="1-2|4|6|8-9"}
library(tidyverse); library(FactoMineR); library(factoextra); library(here)
resp <- read_csv(here("data", "brands.csv"))

tab <- table(resp$brand, resp$attribute)       # the contingency table

chisq.test(tab)$p.value                        # < 0.05 or stop here

ca <- CA(tab, graph = FALSE); round(ca$eig[1:3, 2], 1)
fviz_ca_biplot(ca, repel = TRUE) + labs(title = "Brand perception, 1 200 respondents")
```

Then Drill 2: the four sentences for *this* map.

## [Drill 2]{.drill-kicker} Four sentences for this map

::: {.subtitle-frame}
In pairs · 10 minutes · your `CA(tab)` on `brands.csv`: 4 brands × 5 attributes, 2 356 mentions
:::

| Brand | Dim 1 (84.7%) | Dim 2 (13.4%) | Attribute | Dim 1 | Dim 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | −0.26 | −0.04 | Cheap | 0.93 | 0.20 |
| B | 0.82 | 0.10 | For young people | 0.45 | −0.14 |
| C | −0.07 | −0.27 | Innovative | −0.19 | −0.29 |
| D | −0.48 | 0.26 | Premium | −0.52 | 0.19 |
| | | | Reliable | −0.24 | 0.10 |

1. Write the four sentences for this map: one per axis, one for each of two brands
2. Swap with the pair next to you. Where you disagree, is it the map or the reading?
3. *For young people* was not in this morning's table. Where does it land, and what does it add to B?

## [Drill 2 · answer]{.drill-kicker} The same story, one word richer

- **Axis 1 (85%)**: price — *Cheap* and *For young people* against *Premium* and *Reliable*. B alone on the cheap side, D at the premium end
- **Axis 2 (13%)**: *Innovative* (C) against *Premium* (D) — the two ways of not being cheap, as this morning
- **A** sits near the centre: the average profile with a little more *Reliable* (32% of its mentions, 25% overall). **C** is as close, but along axis 2: the innovative one (32% against 23%)
- **B** owns *cheap* (37% against 14%) and *young* (31% against 18%): youth and price travel together — a position, and a fragile one

[Disagreements are usually a brand-to-attribute "distance" read off the map: check the angle, then the profile.]{.muted}

## A perception map does not tell you where to go. It tells you where you are, and who is standing next to you.  {.statement}
